problem: End-to-end DRL mapless navigation from RGB images spends many network parameters on visual feature extraction, so it needs many samples. Together with the sim-to-real gap, this is why RGB is rarely used as visual input.
motivation: RGB is the most common camera format, but training DRL directly on pixels is sample-inefficient, and DRL needs many interactions that must come from a simulator. Decoupling visual encoding from the policy lets the encoder be trained separately on unlabeled images and reused across environments.
key_idea: Pretrain a VAE to compress the 64x48x3 RGB image into a 32-d latent vector, then feed that latent with the target and previous velocity into a small PPO policy MLP, instead of learning conv features end-to-end.
insight: Separating perception from control improves sample efficiency: the proposed planner reaches an 80% success rate with about 1/4 of the benchmark's samples in maze1 and about 1/3 in maze2 (Figs. 10-11). PPO also clearly beats DQN as the end-to-end baseline and converges more reliably (Fig. 9). Using a VAE rather than a plain autoencoder is motivated by better generalization to unseen, style-like images, but this claim is not ablated.
method: Problem formulation: the policy maps the 64x48x3 RGB image, the 2-d target in polar coordinates (distance, angle) and the previous velocity to a new linear/angular velocity.

E2E baselines: 3 conv layers plus 2 dense layers (512 units) trained end-to-end, with a DQN version (discrete actions; Double DQN, target network, gradient clipping) and a PPO version (continuous velocity).

VAE encoder: 4 stride-2 conv layers (32-64-128-256), dense mu/sigma with 32-d latent z (288x compression), and a deconv decoder. It is trained with MSE reconstruction loss plus KL loss to a unit Gaussian.
VAE training data: 5 million RGB images collected by random-velocity driving in the navigation environment until collision. Trained from scratch with Adam on a GTX 1080Ti; final loss 0.0019.
Motion planner: PPO policy of three 512-unit dense layers taking z (32-d), target (d, alpha) and previous velocity (v, w), outputting linear and angular velocity, with noise added to the actions.

Simulation environments: released Gym-style, ROS-supported mazes (maze1, maze2) with a reward of collision penalty, arrival reward, and distance-difference progress reward minus a per-step time penalty.

setting.backbone: VAE (conv encoder/decoder, from scratch) + 3x512 MLP PPO policy (from scratch)
setting.training_data: 5M random-exploration RGB images from the maze environment for the VAE; PPO trained online by RL in the simulated mazes
setting.observation: monocular RGB 64x48x3 + relative target position (polar) + previous velocity
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity of a nonholonomic robot (DQN baseline uses discrete actions)
setting.simulator: custom Gazebo/ROS maze environments (maze1, maze2) with Gym-style interface
setting.privileged: target relative position (distance and angle) given at test time; no map

numbers_note: Results are given only in figures (average reward and success-rate curves) and text (1/4 and ~1/3 samples to reach 80% success); no numeric tables and no standard benchmark.
results: The VAE+PPO planner reaches the 80% success threshold with roughly 1/4 of the samples of the E2E-PPO benchmark in maze1 and nearly 1/3 in maze2. E2E-PPO in turn clearly outperforms E2E-DQN, which failed to converge in maze2. In maze1 the proposed planner even takes the optimal path in the trajectory example.
limitations: Only evaluated in two self-built simulated mazes, with results in curves only and no real-robot or sim-to-real test despite the motivation.
The VAE is trained on images from the same environment, so generalization to different environments is claimed but not tested, and there is no ablation against a plain AE or other encoders.
Requires ground-truth target position and only compares against the authors' own E2E baselines.
builds_on: Tai et al. virtual-to-real DRL mapless navigation
